newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian museum plans to put Gandhi on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Indian museum plans to put Gandhi on Internet.

text.p: An ambitious project to globalise the man who led India to freedom is quietly taking shape in New Delhi as the country celebrates 50 years of independence from British rule.
The National Gandhi Museum and Library plans to put the works of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, "Mahatma" or great soul to hundreds of millions of Indians, and his pictures on the Internet.
"We want to go on the Internet before the end of this year," the institution's director, Y.P. Anand told Reuters on Friday.
"We are computerising most of the library work. We have more than 10,000 photographs to offer on the Internet," Anand said.
Set up soon after Gandhi's murder at the hands of a Hindu fanatic, the museum houses a vast collection of books, mementoes, personal effects and photographs of the "Father of the Nation".
Clothes Gandhi wore when Nathuram Godse shot him dead five months after India became free, are kept as they are. The blood stains on them have faded into dark patches over time.
"We have with us the pistol and two of the three spent bullets," said Anand. These were not on public view because renovation work was going on in that section, he said.
Far removed from the fashionable part of the capital, the museum stands on the way to Rajghat, the place on the banks of the river Jamuna where Gandhi was cremated.
Facing a dusty highway, close to a smoke-spewing thermal power plant, the museum has had a hard time protecting its priceless possessions.
"We are renovating the museum and air-conditioning it to keep the place free from dust and smoke," Anand said.
He said there had been a surge in demand for photographs of Gandhi and of the freedom movement in the last few weeks as India prepared to celebrate its half a century of independence.
"We must have supplied at least 1,600 photographs last week to various organisations and individuals," Anand said.
Among the pictures there were photos of a half-clad Gandhi joking with an impeccably dressed Mohammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Moslem Pakistan, the mood belying what was in store for posterity.
Pakistan, formed after the partition of pre-independence India, celebrated its 50 years of freedom on Thursday. The two countries have been rivals ever since independence.
"We have come to know a lot about India, just seeing these photographs," said Sibylle Hafner, a medical student from Germany, currently visiting India.
Matthias Vogel, also a German medical student accompanying Hafner, found Gandhi very human.
"His idea of peace and non-violence is appealing, though it's very difficult to put it into practice," Vogel said.
But Gandhi did practice what he preached.

Testimony of this was a walking stick Gandhi used while leading a march in 1930 to the western Indian port town of Dandi in a peaceful protest against the imposition of a tax on salt. The stick was preserved in a glass case at the museum.
